subject: spaceGalley
pitch:
Category: Prop group.
Subject: spaceship galley kitchen.
Style: Alien (1979) Nostromo.
reasoning:
I'm planning a static Nostromo-style galley kitchen prop: counter run with sink, stove, hanging pots, wall panels with switches, and a mess table — all in model space without joints or creatures.

Thinking through the dressing details now: the iconic round mess table with bench seating, grimy off-white and grey-blue surfaces with orange warning accents, CRT monitors, toggle switches, and placeholder labels like "NOSTROMO" and "GALLEY" instead of real logos. I'm sizing the room realistically at about 4m wide by 3m deep by 2.4m high, with a grated floor deck, a back wall and one side wall forming a corner, and a partial ceiling with hanging pipes, leaving the front and one side open toward the viewer.

I'm skipping joints entirely since static models can omit them, and planning helper functions for boxes and cylinders to position parts in model space, along with a worn industrial color palette of dirty beige, off-white, dark grey-blue, and warning yellow-orange tones.

I'm pulling panel and metal materials from a clockwork kit and designing a custom grime paint that darkens near floors and ceilings with noise-based streaks. For surface textures I'm planning SVGs for hazard signage, a glowing control panel with switches and indicator lights, a CRT screen with green scrolling text, a Nostromo schematic poster, and a cabinet door.

I'm also sketching out additional texture needs like a stove burner plate, pipe labels, fridge panels, a diamond-plate floor grating pattern with yellow hazard borders, and a menu board/clock screen, aiming for roughly six to eight total. Then I'm starting to lay out scene elements, beginning with the floor slab dimensions and its grating paint, raised deck plates, and the back wall panel.

Now I'm defining the left wall paneling with vertical ribs and figuring out the ceiling structure—rather than a full slab that would block the view from above, I'm planning a bulkhead frame of cross-beams with recessed glowing light panels between them.

For the back wall I'm adding a full counter run: cabinets, a steel countertop with a sunken sink basin and swan-neck faucet, a stove with four ring burners and a glowing extractor hood venting to the ceiling, overhead shelves with mugs and jars, control panels, a microwave/oven, coffee machine, hanging utensil rack, and pots on hooks with pans already on the stove.

Now I'm working on the left wall with tall fridge/freezer lockers, each with handles and labels, plus maybe a bulkhead door with a round window and a monitor on a swing arm. In the center I'm placing the long mess table with six bolted stools, scattered trays, mugs, a bowl labeled "JONES" for the cat, a coffee pot, bottles, generic labeled cans, and I'm considering adding the iconic drinking bird toy as a nostalgic detail.

Now I'm adding the drinking bird's pivoting stand on the table, overhead pipes with red valve wheels running along the ceiling and back corner, a CRT monitor bracket glowing green on the back wall, hanging cables, yellow-black hazard stripes along floor edges and door frames, a trash chute hatch, and a handle rail. I'm aiming for roughly 200-300 parts and 5-12 textures, estimating the code will land around 600-800 lines, and I need to be extra careful about correctness since I can't test it directly.

Working through part orientations...

Setting up a box helper function and thinking about the Paint/color type import from the builder module.

Now I'm sketching helper functions for placing slabs and cylinders along different axes, then planning out the SVG textures for cabinet doors with panel colors and recessed borders.

I'm also tallying the full texture set needed—door variants, hazard stripes, switch panels, CRT, signage, labels—keeping the count manageable for the atlas, and deciding doors should be thin textured boxes or planes rather than fully textured carcasses.

Now I'm working out the precise room coordinates: wall positions and thicknesses for back and left walls, and the floor's extents, center, and width to make sure everything aligns without gaps.

I'm working out how the back and left walls overlap at the corner so their volumes nest without z-fighting, with the back wall spanning the full width and the left wall's inner face tucked inside it. The right end (x=-2.3) stays open as an edge rather than adding a bulkhead there.

For wall paneling, I'm designing a panelled grime shader that lays out a grid based on the dominant face, using 0.6-wide panels with rivets at 0.1 pitch, and painting a base that darkens toward floor and ceiling with grime noise and streaking. I'm settling on a Nostromo-style color scheme: warm grey-beige panels with a cool dark teal-grey wainscot band below y<0.95.

Writing the wall color function...

Now for the floor, I'm thinking through a diamond grating pattern with hazard-striped edges and seam lines every 0.6m, while estimating total texel density across the roughly 80 square meters of painted surfaces to decide texture resolution.

I'm bumping paintSize up to 2048 to get finer detail around 5mm per texel, which handles the thin panel seams and grating better. Now I'm laying out a back-wall counter run spanning 3.6m, with a recessed plinth base, cabinet body, and countertop slab.

I'm dividing the counter into six 0.6m-wide door modules—assigning drawers, a sink unit, a stove with oven window, and plain doors across the span, with door faces set just proud of the cabinet front plane.

Now I'm adding handle bars as thin steel rods across each door and splitting the countertop into segments to leave a gap for the sink basin, which I'll sink in as a dark steel box recessed below the counter surface.

For the basin I'm building four thin walls plus a dark bottom and a drain disk, then shaping a swan-neck faucet using a catmull curve that arcs up from the base near the wall and sweeps down over the basin opening.

Now I'm laying out the stove hob with a black plate on the counter and four burner discs, adding torus rings for glowing burners and thin cross-bar grates, then sketching pots with a lathe profile to give them hollow bodies sitting on two of the burners.

Above the stove I'm placing an extractor hood built from a trapezoidal frustum shape narrowing toward the ceiling, connected to a duct box running up to the ceiling, all finished in steel paint.

Then I'm adding a backsplash panel behind the counter and floating shelves on the left wall, each with a front lip, and populating them with simple canned goods built from cylinders with wraparound label colors.

I'm sketching jars, mugs with torus handles, and ration boxes to populate the shelves, then turning to lockers on the right wall split into three tall units.

For the lockers, I'm planning three carcasses fit beside the counter—fridge with handle and display, freezer, and dry store—spacing their centers so they fit the depth and z-range available without overlapping the counter run, with each door positioned as a plane on the inner-facing side.

Working out the door plane orientation math...

Both axis cases check out consistently with how lookAt orients the +Z face, so the texture should read correctly from the viewer's side. Now adding details above the locker—ducts, a vent grille—and a steel handle rod on the fridge door's hinge side.

For the mess table, I'm placing it in the open floor space with a layout echoing the Nostromo's long table: two pedestal legs with base plates supporting a rounded-corner tabletop, extruded as a flat slab at seated height.

Now I'm laying out the six stools with their cylindrical stalks and lathed orange vinyl seats, positioning them symmetrically on both sides of the table, then moving on to the table items like trays built from grey compartmentalized boxes.

For small props I'm adding mugs, a glass coffee pot with a dark amber lathe shape and black handle, and a cat bowl -- skipping the "JONES" text idea since it feels awkward on the geometry and instead giving the bowl a simple pink interior disc for kibble. I'm also starting on the drinking bird toy, building its box base, rod legs, pivot axle, and a red glass sphere for the lower bulb.

Finishing the bird's glass head with a pale blue neck tube, sphere head, cone beak, and a lathe-built top hat with a red feather, plus a small water cup positioned in front. Then I'm planning the hanging pot rack over the counter—a ceiling rail with hooks and utensils dangling down, positioned to avoid the hood and align with the shelf heights.

Working out the wall-mounted bracket rods holding the rail, and building the hanging utensils: a swept ladle with lathe bowl, an extruded spatula, and a pan made from a lathe profile reoriented to face outward with a disc base and hollow interior, hung by its handle hole.

Reworking the layout to avoid conflicts: shelves confined to x -2.0 to -0.95 at two heights, rail spanning x -2.05 to -0.4 for hanging items, with hanging utensils and a pot placed at x -0.85, -0.65, -0.5, and -0.7 respectively to keep clear of the extractor hood near x -0.25.

Now positioning the ladle, spatula, and pan on the rail to avoid overlapping each other and the hood, then planning a system panel with glowing toggles and lamps plus a small CRT monitor on a bracket to the right of the hood on the back wall.

Actually, I'm refining the CRT monitor placement to the top counter's right end as a chunky retro unit with a rear frustum and glowing green screen text, an Alien-style touch, alongside a coffee machine and a gap left open for a spice rack, with the wall panel positioned above both.

For the ceiling, I'm adding structural beams spaced across the width at regular z intervals, with longitudinal beams running perpendicular, and placing a few glowing downward-facing light panels between them plus an additional light box near the table.

Now I'm routing overhead pipes along the ceiling edges at different depths, using steel and copper-toned coloring with ring-shaped clamps, and adding a vertical corner pipe with a torus-shaped valve wheel running floor to ceiling.

Checking the pipe placement overlaps with the shifted locker positions, I adjust locker centers to -1.0, -0.2, 0.6 so the pipe at z -1.53 clears the corner locker, leaving a small but workable gap with the counter edge. Now I'm thinking about left-wall details above the lockers—ducts and a bulkhead hatch door positioned higher up around z 1.1 to 1.8.

I want to add an oval hatch door at the far wall with hazard stripe texturing and a small window, labeled something like "MESS DECK ACCESS." I'll also run some thick black cable sweeps from ceiling to panel along the walls, and add a structural column stub near x -2.25 to break up the right-edge wall.

Then I'm layering in smaller details: a recessed intercom speaker on the back wall, a small waste bin near the table, and a couple of ration crates stacked near the right-front floor area. Finally I'll add a "GALLEY" sign stencil above the doorway on the back wall.

I'm sketching out the texture list I'll need: cabinet door panels, drawers, oven, fridge/freezer/dry-store variants, switch panels, a CRT screen, signage, and a hatch door texture.

For hazard striping, I'll skip a dedicated texture and instead handle it procedurally with painted diagonal stripes on surfaces like column bases, using an amber-and-black stripe pattern. I'm also planning to frame the hatch door with a few boxes to form its surrounding border.

For the floor paint, I'm writing a function that checks surface normals and position to darken the base color, add diagonal hazard stripes along the front edge near the hatch, and generate a subtle grating pattern using fractional UV coordinates to create dark recessed holes.

Now I'm defining the metal and paint materials: steel and iron for the hood and fittings, brass for accents, a grimy off-white for the cabinet bodies, and dark seam lines every 0.75 units across the floor plates to suggest panel joints.

I'll need to keep the flat color palette under 64 distinct values since paints don't count against that limit. For the actual construction, I'm sketching helper functions for placing geometry: a cylinder helper that takes position, radius, height, color, and axis, plus a direction mapping for aiming parts along x, y, or z axes using the part system's `at`, `dir`, and `rotation` properties.

I'm also planning sphere, rod, sweep, and lathe helpers — the rod connects two points with a given radius and color, sweep follows a polyline path, and lathe revolves a 2D outline (with x ≥ 0) around an axis to build solid shapes like a mug, starting from the outline definition.

For the handle, I'm shaping a half-torus and rotating it so the arc bulges outward on the correct side of the mug, working through the rotation math to get the handle facing the right direction.

Now I'm setting up helper functions for generating the SVG textures — a text stencil helper and a cabinet texture function for rendering door and drawer styles.

Adding more furniture pieces...

Better to skip texture-drawn lamps and use actual 3D glow elements plus physical toggle switches and ball joints placed on a plain panel, mapping SVG coordinates to world offsets so each control lines up correctly. Now I'm moving on to designing the CRT screen texture with a black background base.

Writing SVG code...

I'll settle on 12 textures total: doors, drawers, oven, lockers, panel, crt, sign, hatch, plaque. Now I'm setting up the scene constants — floor height, wall positions, ceiling — and starting to place the floor and back wall boxes.

Adding wall trim details...

Positioning the vertical wall ribs and catching a z-fighting issue with the panel, so I'm nudging the panel and rib depths slightly apart to avoid overlap.

Dropping the back wall ribs idea, I'll instead add ceiling beams spaced along the z-axis plus a longitudinal beam and corner columns for structure, then start placing light fixtures between the beams.

I'm settling on roughly four to six fixtures with a glow strength around 1.3, checking that they fit within the gaps between beams. I'm also planning a ceiling plate positioned only above the counter region to anchor the hood duct and pipes, sizing it around 4.6 by 0.9 with its center near y 2.62 and z -1.35.

Now I'm routing the back pipes carefully to avoid colliding with the beams and hood duct, adjusting their z and y positions and radii — one larger pipe around y 2.38 below the beam bottom, and a thinner copper pipe nearby, while double-checking the duct box doesn't intersect them.

I'm also figuring out the clamp rings every 0.9m along the pipes, and tracing a vertical pipe near x=1.95 up to an elbow joint, but realizing the horizontal connection point at z=-1.35 would run straight through the locker's footprint, so I need to reroute it.

Moving the horizontal pipe and its vertical counterpart to z=-1.5 so they clear both the locker and the ceiling beam, then adding a valve wheel partway up the vertical pipe and checking its torus geometry doesn't clip into anything nearby.

Another gas pipe runs yellow at r.045 from z -1.5 to 1.8. Then I'm working out the hood duct geometry rising from the stove hood to the ceiling, positioning the box and frustum dimensions so it aligns with the hood below without clipping the wall.

Now I'm laying out the counter module positions along x at six evenly spaced centers of width .6 each, then building the cabinet carcass, kicker plate, and countertop segments as boxes with specific sizes and offsets so the countertop extends flush to the wall.

I'm working out the sink gap geometry: splitting the countertop into two main segments around a sink opening, then adding thin lip pieces at the front and back of that gap to frame where the sink would sit.

Now I'm placing the faucet near the back lip so its spout arcs forward over the opening, and sketching out the basin itself—a shallow dark steel box with side walls set inward from the opening edges.

I realize there's a conflict: the carcass body solid fills up to y 0.93, which would completely bury the basin bottom at 0.79 inside solid geometry, making it invisible. I need to split the carcass into separate boxes so the basin cavity stays open and visible underneath the countertop.

Working out the door plane is hidden by the carcass gap, so the left and right carcasses (widths .6 and 2.4) frame a basin gap of .52, with the void underneath concealed by the basin walls when viewed from above. For the doors, I'm positioning them at the front face with a center height of .54 and size .54×.7 to match the carcass opening.

Now I'm assigning door textures per module (drawers, two door styles, oven) and adding 3D handle geometry—vertical bars for doors, horizontal bars for drawer fronts—plus placing the stovetop hob plate as a dark box sitting above the countertop.

Still building the stove details...

Now placing pots on burners - a lathed pot shape on one burner and a saucepan with a handle facing forward on another, plus sink-area extras like a sponge, detergent bottle, and a dish rack with plates to the left of the sink.

For the dish rack, I'm giving it a wire base box with five thin cylindrical plates standing upright side by side, discs facing sideways, colored off-white, positioned near the counter edge. To the right of the stove I'm adding a utensil holder pot.

I'm also adding a cutting board with a wood-colored flat box and a knife on top made from a silver blade and dark handle, plus a coffee machine with a dark steel body, spout, glass carafe, drip tray, and a glowing green status LED, carefully positioning the carafe just under the spout so it fits beneath the body without overlapping awkwardly.

Now I'm setting up the machine's base plate so the pot rests on it, then building the upper arm and head sections that overhang the carafe. After that I'm moving on to the CRT, starting with its front body box and a tapered rear section to give it that classic boxy monitor shape.

Still working out bezel and screen sizing...

I'm placing a dark backing panel on the wall with a plane front for toggles and lamp glow discs, checking clearances against the CRT top. Then I'm positioning a small plaque to the right of the panel on the back wall, working out its x,y coordinates relative to the panel's span.

Now I'm trying to fit a sign above shelves on the left wall, but it keeps colliding with a vertical pipe and a hanging rail at similar heights, so I'm nudging its y-position and size to avoid overlap while keeping it above the shelf items.

Instead I decide to relocate the sign above a hatch door on the left wall near z=1.45, checking that the pipe placement still clears it, and then I work out the hatch door's frame and center dimensions.

I'll extend the floor and walls depth-wise so the hatch posts clear the lockers, centering the hatch at z=1.55 with door width .76 giving posts at 1.14 and 1.96. I'm also adjusting the door plane to sit flush but slightly recessed from the frame, letting the frame posts protrude a bit like trim, then checking clearance around the mess table near the hatch/locker area.

Checking that stool positions stay clear of the counter front and locker bank, I'm now working out the table's structure: a top surface slab, two pedestal columns with base and top plates, and three stools offset along the z-axis from the table center.

Now I'm designing each stool's seat, stalk, and base plate dimensions, then adding a small footrest ring attached via radial struts to the stalk for support. With six stools total these small geometric loops should stay cheap to render, and I'm starting to lay out table items like trays relative to the tabletop height.

Continuing the table setup, I'm placing a food tray with compartments made from scaled sphere "blobs" for food, a second rotated tray, a scattering of mugs, a coffee pot built from a lathe shape with a dark glass body and black base, a white lathe bowl for the cat, and a drinking bird figure positioned nearby.

For the bird, I'm working out a manual tilt calculation to make it lean forward toward a water cup, as if drinking, by rotating its local coordinate points around a pivot axis rather than building a jointed structure.

Now I'm filling out the scene extras: a ketchup bottle with small salt and pepper shakers, a couple of cans, and skipping cutlery and napkin dispensers. For the floor, I'm placing crates, a grey trash can with an orange stripe and lid near the counter's left end, checking clearances with the stools and table so nothing overlaps.

I'm adding a stack of three yellow-grey crates with strap details near the counter corner, plus a bulkhead support post with a hazard-striped band at its base along the left wall.

Now I'm working out a hanging utensil rail suspended from steel rods with brackets along the shelving, checking that items like a ladle don't collide with the shelf depth and other hanging objects.

Adding the hanging pot with its hook, then laying out two shelves with lip trim and brackets, stocked with cans, jars, boxes, and mugs to fill out the kitchen scene.

Now I'm weighing where to place a wall-mounted extinguisher for a pop of red, checking clearances near the locker, pipe, and counter before settling on the left wall near the hatch posts.

Actually, rejecting that spot for clearance issues, I decide to mount the extinguisher against the column instead, facing outward with a small lathe-built cylinder and nozzle, confirming it clears the counter edge. I'm also planning a drooping cable running from a ceiling beam down to a panel using a catmull curve for natural sag.

Then I add a second cable segment behind the CRT monitor to the wall for extra detail, and start considering a ventilation grille on the left wall above the lockers, positioning a vent duct box in the gap between the locker tops and the ceiling beam.

Actually, I realize the yellow pipe I'd placed conflicts with this duct, so I decide to drop the pipe and simplify, making the duct the main ceiling feature with flange bands and a grilled front face built from boxes.

Now I'm adding a few thin dark slats to the duct's face, skipping extras like a cat-flap or bulkhead door, and setting up a seeded random helper plus a flat color palette (steel, dark, black, cream, beige, orange, red) before writing the actual scene code.

Defining box and cylinder helper functions...

Still writing helper functions...

Writing paint functions for grime and wall textures...

Still writing wall shading logic...

Defining materials for cab, floor, and hazard stripes using coordinate-based diagonal patterns, plus an orange vinyl paint that blends two colors based on surface normal with grime overlay.

For the table top I'm creating a cream laminate texture with subtle ring stains, adding an orange inlay border near the extruded edges, and coloring the side walls dark metal where the normal tilts away from vertical. Now moving on to write the door textures.

Still writing SVG code...

Writing locker door and panel texture code...

Writing hatch texture details...

Now I'm planning the full build function structure—setting up the builder, helpers, and shell geometry for the galley scene.

Writing shell geometry code...

Adding floor paint logic...

Defining counter cabinet dimensions...

Adding the hob plate positioned on the countertop with black coloring and glow rings, then moving on to structure the shelf item loops by height level.

Still writing shelf items...

Actually I'll orient the pan so the shiny bottom faces outward toward viewers, keeping the interior hidden for a more natural hanging look. Now I'm working out the spatula shape—a handle rod extending down into a flat blade outline, figuring out the orientation vectors so the blade hangs correctly below the handle.

Next I'm designing the ladle: a handle rod dropping down into a half-sphere bowl, considering whether to use a lathe or a sliced sphere geometry to get the right scoop shape facing forward.

Still writing lathe geometry...

I'm estimating total part counts across all the furniture groups, landing around 300 boxes overall, and sketching out the locker bank layout with carcass dimensions split across three z-positions.

Still writing locker details...

I'll simplify — skip the glow plane and just render the temperature readout as bright green text on black directly in the texture, no emissive effects needed. I should also add small LED dots nearby for detail, plus locker vents on the cab's left wall. For more Nostromo atmosphere, I'm considering a tall narrow wall light strip and additional monitors.

Now setting up the type definitions and helper structures for building parts—defining vector types, axis mappings, and a flexible options interface for boxes, textures, and glow effects, using `any` where strict typing would be overly restrictive. Writing part constructors...

Adding toggle lever geometry and colors...

Now I'm adding the coffee pot details and moving to the stool and table geometry—setting up the tabletop extrusion with bevels and smoothing, and reconsidering whether smoothing level 2 makes sense for a rectangle without sharp corners.

Still writing bird geometry...

Still building bird details...

Confirming the rng helper is callable as expected, then writing the fire extinguisher as a lathe shape with a rounded nozzle profile, colored red and positioned near the column.

Checking placement clearances for the extinguisher, trash bin, and crates relative to the counter and walls to make sure nothing overlaps.

Now I'm figuring out crate details - stacking a smaller rotated crate on top with strap handles and a yellow stencil stripe, then moving on to the hood frustum geometry with its width and height transitions before finalizing and returning the root object.

Adding more fixtures...

Adding more pipe details...
